lessons.title: Why you make things
lessons.summary: What creative work is for, and the difference between making and performing for an audience.
objectives: You will say who your work is for
You will describe one piece that moved you and why
You will name what you want to be good at
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Discuss: who is this for, and what should it do to them?
- Each person describes one piece of work that moved them
- Write what you want to be able to do by the end of the term

## Understand it

Every piece of creative work — a song, a play, a painting, a dance, a film — is made **for someone** and is meant to **do something to them**: make them laugh, think, remember, dance, feel less alone, see something differently. Artists who know their purpose make clearer choices.

Two questions to ask of any work, yours or anyone's:

1. **Who is it for?** A child, a congregation, a festival crowd, your grandmother, people who share your experience, people who do not?
2. **What should it do to them?** Not "be good" — something specific: *make them want to dance*, *make them angry about an injustice*, *make them proud of where they come from*.

Think of a piece of work that **moved you**. Describe it precisely: what was it, where did you meet it, and **what exactly did it do to you**? Then — the useful part — **how** did it do it? A sudden silence? A face in close-up? A lyric that named something you had never heard said aloud?

This is how artists learn from other artists: not by copying the surface, but by understanding the **effect** and the **means**.

**Setting a goal for the term:** write one concrete thing you want to be able to do by the end — "perform a full song without stopping", "finish a short film with clear sound", "hold a scene with real listening". A goal you can check is one you can work towards.

## Key words

- **Audience:** the people a work is made for
- **Intent:** what the artist wants the work to do
- **Means:** the techniques that create an effect

## Read and watch

- [The danger of a single story](https://www.ted.com/talks/chimamanda_ngozi_adichie_the_danger_of_a_single_story) — Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie (TED)
- [Pixar in a Box](https://www.khanacademy.org/computing/pixar) — Khan Academy with Pixar

## Practise at home

1. Write your aim in one sentence and keep it
1. Find one piece of work you admire and write why

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work small and finish it. A finished small thing teaches you more than an unfinished ambitious one.
- **If you already can:** Take the same brief and make a second, different answer to it, then say which is stronger and why.

lessons.title: How skill is actually built
lessons.summary: Deliberate practice: short, specific, uncomfortable and repeated, rather than long and vague.
objectives: You will break a skill into one specific weakness
You will practise only that for ten minutes
You will say why repeating what you can already do is not practice
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Name one thing you cannot yet do in your craft
- Practise only that, slowly, for ten minutes
- Learn the difference between practising and performing

```steps 10 Warm up | 15 One named weakness | 35 New material | 40 Put it together | 20 Show and take notes
```

## Understand it

Most people practise by **doing what they can already do** — playing their favourite song, drawing the face they draw well. It feels good and it builds very little. Research on how experts develop, led by the psychologist **K. Anders Ericsson**, describes something different, called **deliberate practice**:

- **One specific weakness at a time** — not "get better at guitar" but "change cleanly from G to C in time".
- **Just beyond your current ability** — hard enough to fail sometimes, not so hard you cannot do it at all.
- **Slow and correct** — speed comes from accurate repetition; fast mistakes are practised mistakes.
- **Immediate feedback** — a teacher, a recording, a mirror, a metronome tells you at once whether it worked.
- **Full concentration**, for limited time — short, focused sessions beat long distracted ones. Ten minutes of real focus is worth an hour of noodling.
- **Repetition, spread over days** — sleep consolidates skills; daily short practice beats one weekly marathon.

**Practising is not performing.** In practice, you stop, isolate, slow down and repeat the hard part. In performance, you go straight through and never stop. Both are skills — and mixing them up hurts both. Many people "practise" by running the whole piece again and again, repeating the same mistakes each time.

The practice cycle: **name the problem → slow it down → repeat it correctly → check → speed up slightly → put it back in context**.

## Key words

- **Deliberate practice:** focused practice on a specific weakness with feedback
- **Feedback:** information on whether something worked
- **Consolidation:** skills settling into memory, especially during sleep

## Read and watch

- [Grit: the power of passion and perseverance](https://www.ted.com/talks/angela_lee_duckworth_grit_the_power_of_passion_and_perseverance) — Angela Lee Duckworth (TED)
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Ten minutes a day on one named weakness, nothing else
1. Write down the weakness and what changed

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work small and finish it. A finished small thing teaches you more than an unfinished ambitious one.
- **If you already can:** Take the same brief and make a second, different answer to it, then say which is stronger and why.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Looking and listening properly
lessons.summary: Critique: giving it usefully, and taking it without defending.
objectives: You will give a specific critique with evidence
You will take a critique without explaining yourself
You will say why "I like it" is useless
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn the shape: what you saw, what it did, one thing to try
- Take a critique in silence, write it down, then say thank you
- Practise on two classmates' work

## Understand it

A **critique** (crit) is how artists help each other improve. Done well, it is the fastest way to see your work as others see it. Done badly — "I like it", "it's boring" — it helps nobody, and can hurt.

**A shape that works:**

1. **What you saw/heard** — describe, without judging. "The song starts with only the voice; the drums come in at the chorus."
2. **What it did to you** — the effect, honestly. "The drums arriving made me feel lifted." or "I lost interest in the second verse."
3. **One thing to try** — a specific, practical suggestion. "What if the second verse dropped the guitar too?"

This works because it separates **observation** (which the maker cannot argue with), **response** (which is your honest experience) and **suggestion** (which the maker is free to take or leave).

**Receiving critique:**

- **Listen in silence.** Do not explain or defend — you will not be there to explain when an audience sees it.
- **Write it down** — you will forget, and you will remember the hurtful bits more than the useful ones.
- Say **"thank you"** — they gave you their attention.
- **Decide later** what to act on. You do not have to take every suggestion; but if three people say the same thing, it is probably true.

Looking and listening carefully, without rushing to judge, is itself an artistic skill.

## Key words

- **Critique:** structured feedback on creative work
- **Observation:** describing what is there, without judgement
- **Suggestion:** a specific idea the maker may try

## Read and watch

- [Giving feedback](https://www.mindtools.com/a0edu3n/giving-feedback) — Mind Tools
- [GCSE Drama](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zbckjxs) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Practise receiving without defending

lessons.title: Where you are making from
lessons.summary: Nigerian creative heritage, and why the work in front of you has a history.
objectives: You will name three Nigerian artists or traditions in your field
You will connect one to what you make
You will say why copying a foreign model uncritically is weak work
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Research three figures or traditions in your own discipline
- Find one thing in your own work that connects
- Discuss: work rooted in somewhere is stronger than work rooted in nowhere

## Understand it

No artist makes from nowhere. Every work grows out of **traditions** — of a place, a people, a discipline — even when it breaks with them. Knowing your roots gives your work depth, and gives you something no one else has.

Nigeria has extraordinary creative traditions to draw on:

- **Theatre and literature** — Hubert Ogunde, Duro Ladipo, **Wole Soyinka** (Nobel Prize, 1986), Chinua Achebe, Femi Osofisan, Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie.
- **Music** — jùjú (King Sunny Adé), fújì, highlife (Rex Lawson, Victor Olaiya), **Afrobeat** (Fela Kuti and Tony Allen), gospel, Afrobeats.
- **Visual art** — the **Nok** terracottas (over 2,000 years old), **Ife** bronze and terracotta heads, the **Benin** bronzes and ivories, the Oshogbo school, Ben Enwonwu, Bruce Onobrakpeya, El Anatsui.
- **Textiles and craft** — adire, aso oke, akwete, beadwork.
- **Film** — Nollywood, one of the largest film industries in the world.

Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's talk *The danger of a single story* argues that when people only hear one story about a place, they misunderstand it. Artists who tell the **specific** stories of their own places help correct that.

**Research three figures or traditions** in your own discipline. For each: what did they make, what was new about it, and what can you take from it? Then find **one thing in your own work** that connects to them — a rhythm, a theme, a technique, a way of telling.

## Key words

- **Tradition:** practices passed down within a culture or discipline
- **Influence:** the effect earlier work has on new work
- **Nok:** an ancient Nigerian culture known for terracotta sculpture

## Read and watch

- [The danger of a single story](https://www.ted.com/talks/chimamanda_ngozi_adichie_the_danger_of_a_single_story) — Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie (TED)
- [Art of Africa](https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/art-africa) — Khan Academy
- [Wole Soyinka: Nobel Prize facts](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/1986/soyinka/facts/) — The Nobel Prize

## Practise at home

1. Research one more and write three sentences
1. Find one local influence you can use

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work small and finish it. A finished small thing teaches you more than an unfinished ambitious one.
- **If you already can:** Take the same brief and make a second, different answer to it, then say which is stronger and why.

lessons.title: Working to a brief
lessons.summary: Somebody else decides what is needed, and you still make it good.
objectives: You will read a brief and list its constraints
You will make something inside them
You will say why constraints help
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Take a brief and list every constraint: time, materials, audience, length
- Make something that meets all of them
- Notice that the constraints made deciding easier

## Understand it

Professional creative work almost always starts with a **brief** — a description of what is needed: a song for a wedding, a poster for an event, a three-minute play for a school, a dance for a festival opening.

A good brief states the **constraints**:

- **Purpose** — what it must achieve.
- **Audience** — who it is for.
- **Length or size** — 3 minutes, A3, 30 seconds.
- **Deadline** — when it must be finished.
- **Budget and materials** — what you can use.
- **Must-haves and must-nots** — a logo, a theme, no profanity, the client's colours.

**Constraints are useful, not just limits.** Faced with "make anything", most people freeze. A tight brief removes thousands of decisions and points you towards a solution. Many great works were made to strict limits: a three-minute single, a fourteen-line sonnet, a commission for one space.

**Working to a brief:**

1. **List every constraint** before you begin.
2. **Ask questions** where anything is unclear — before, not after.
3. **Generate several ideas** quickly, then choose the strongest against the brief.
4. **Check against the brief** during and at the end — does it do everything required?
5. **Deliver on time**. A good piece that is late often fails the brief.

Notice how much easier the decisions became once the constraints were clear.

## Key words

- **Brief:** a description of what a piece of work must achieve
- **Constraint:** a limit the work must meet — time, length, budget
- **Commission:** a piece of work made to order, usually paid

## Read and watch

- [Design thinking](https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/design-thinking) — Interaction Design Foundation

lessons.title: Rehearsal
lessons.summary: Doing it again, and again, until it holds up when you are nervous.
objectives: You will rehearse one piece to a schedule
You will run it start to finish without stopping
You will say why stopping at every mistake is a bad habit
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Rehearse with a plan, not by playing favourite bits
- Run it once start to finish, mistakes and all
- Practise carrying on after a mistake — that is the skill on the night

## Understand it

**Rehearsal** turns material you know into a performance you can rely on. Many performers waste rehearsals by playing their favourite bits over and over while the hard parts stay hard.

**Rehearse with a plan:**

- Start each session with a **goal**: "the transition into the second scene", "the last chorus", "the entrance and first line".
- **Work the hardest parts first**, while you are fresh.
- **Isolate** problems — rehearse a difficult four bars or a tricky exchange many times, slowly, then put it back into context.
- **Note** what changed and what still needs work.

**Run-throughs** — the whole piece, start to finish, without stopping — are a different and essential kind of rehearsal:

- They build **stamina** and show how the parts connect.
- They reveal **where you get lost** or tired.
- Most importantly, they train you to **keep going after a mistake** — the skill that matters most on the night. Audiences forgive mistakes they barely notice; they notice when a performer stops.

**Recovering from mistakes** in rehearsal on purpose: if you slip, find the next secure point (the next line, the next bar, the next move) and carry on. Practise this deliberately.

The last rehearsals should be **as close to the real thing as possible**: in the space, at full energy, in costume or kit, ideally with someone watching.

## Key words

- **Rehearsal:** practising a performance in preparation
- **Run-through:** performing the whole piece without stopping
- **Recovery:** carrying on smoothly after a mistake

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Drama](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zbckjxs) — BBC Bitesize
- [RSC education resources](https://www.rsc.org.uk/education) — Royal Shakespeare Company

## Practise at home

1. Daily full run-through, no stopping
1. One section practised slowly, separately

lessons.title: Critiquing your own earlier work
lessons.summary: Returning to what you made in week 5 with the eyes you have now.
objectives: You will critique your own week 5 work in the week 3 shape
You will name one thing to change
You will make that change
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Look at your week 5 work as if it were someone else's
- Write the critique in the proper shape
- Make the one change you named

## Understand it

One of the hardest and most useful skills an artist has is looking at their **own** work honestly — as if a stranger had made it.

A little distance helps: two weeks after week 5, you are not as attached to the choices you made. You see the work more as an audience will.

**Critique yourself in the proper shape** (from week 3):

1. **What is there** — describe it neutrally.
2. **What it does** — honestly, as an audience member: where did your attention drift? Where did it land?
3. **One thing to try** — a specific change.

Avoid two traps:

- **Too harsh** — "it's all rubbish" gives you nothing to work on, and stops you making.
- **Too kind** — defending every choice because you made it.

Then **make the one change you named** — and only that one. Keep **both versions**. Comparing them teaches you whether your judgement was right: sometimes the change is a clear improvement, sometimes not — and that tells you something too.

Many artists keep a **process journal**: what they tried, what they changed, why. Over months it becomes a record of how your taste and skill grew — and a source of ideas when you are stuck.

## Key words

- **Self-critique:** judging your own work honestly
- **Distance:** time away that lets you see work freshly
- **Process journal:** a record of decisions and changes in your work

## Read and watch

- [Giving feedback](https://www.mindtools.com/a0edu3n/giving-feedback) — Mind Tools
- [Design thinking](https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/design-thinking) — Interaction Design Foundation

1. Make the change and keep both versions
1. Ask someone which is better and why

lessons.title: In front of people
lessons.summary: Nerves, presence and the first ten seconds.
objectives: You will use a settling routine before performing
You will hold the first ten seconds without rushing
You will finish properly instead of fleeing
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn a breathing routine and use it before you start
- Walk on, settle, breathe, then begin — do not rush the start
- Finish, hold, acknowledge, then leave

## Understand it

Performing or presenting in front of people triggers the body's alarm system: adrenaline, fast heart, shallow breath, shaking hands, dry mouth. This is normal — professionals feel it too. The aim is to **manage** it, so it becomes energy rather than panic.

**A breathing routine** before you start:

- Breathe **in for 4** counts, **out for 6–8**. A longer out-breath slows the heart.
- Repeat four or five times. Feel your feet on the floor.

**The shape of a performance — a ritual you can rely on:**

1. **Walk on** with purpose; do not hurry.
2. **Settle** — take your position, find your stillness.
3. **Breathe** — one slow breath.
4. **Begin** — do not rush the start. A moment of calm stillness reads as confidence.
5. **Finish** — hold the last moment; do not run off on the last note or word.
6. **Acknowledge** — a bow, a nod, a "thank you". Accept applause; it is part of the event.
7. **Leave** — calmly.

**During:** focus on the work and what it should do to the audience, not on yourself. If you make a mistake, carry on — the audience usually does not know what was meant to happen.

**Preparation is the real cure**: when the material is secure through rehearsal and run-throughs, nerves have less to grab on to.

## Key words

- **Stage fright:** anxiety before or during performance
- **Ritual:** a fixed routine that steadies the performer
- **Presence:** calm, focused energy that holds an audience

1. Practise your settling routine every time

- Discuss: credit is how creative people get hired and paid

## Understand it

Almost all serious creative work is **collaborative**: a film needs dozens of people; a song may have writers, a producer, musicians and an engineer; a play has actors, a director, designers and crew. Learning to work with others — and to **credit** them properly — is a professional skill.

**Collaborating well:**

- **Agree roles** at the start — who decides what? (Director decides staging; designer decides costume, within the director's vision.)
- **Share the idea, not just tasks** — everyone should know what the piece is trying to do.
- **Disagree about the work, not the person** — "I think this scene is too long", not "you always overdo it".
- **Meet deadlines** — others depend on your part.

**Credit** is how creative people **get hired and paid**. A credit list records who did what:

- **Full names** (spelled correctly), and their **role** — "Writer", "Director", "Camera", "Sound", "Costume", "Performer".
- **Everyone** who contributed, including people who lent equipment or a location.
- For music, songwriting credits decide who earns **royalties**.

**Using others' work:** music, images, footage and writing belong to their creators. Use only what you have permission for, what you made, or what is openly licensed — such as **Creative Commons** — and credit it as the licence requires. Copyright in Nigeria and most of the world exists automatically when a work is created.

## Key words

- **Collaboration:** making work together, with shared purpose
- **Credit:** public acknowledgement of who did what
- **Copyright:** the creator's legal right over their work
- **Creative Commons:** licences that let creators share work on stated terms

objectives: You will photograph or record three pieces properly

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Record or photograph three pieces in good light
- Caption each: what, when, your role, what it was for
- Store them somewhere you will still have in two years

## Understand it

A **portfolio** is a collection of your best work, documented so others can see what you can do. It is how artists get places on courses, commissions, jobs and gigs. Work that is not documented, as far as the world is concerned, did not happen.

**Documenting work well:**

- **Light** — photograph artwork and objects in soft daylight (by a window, not in direct sun), with no flash glare. Photograph flat work square-on to avoid distortion.
- **Video and audio** — steady camera (a tripod or a stack of books), clean sound (close to the source, quiet room).
- **Plain background** — let the work be the subject.
- **Several angles** for 3D work, plus a detail shot.

**Caption every piece:**

- **What** it is (title, medium — "Adire eleko on cotton", "Original song, vocals and guitar").
- **When** it was made.
- **Your role** — especially in group work ("Director and editor").
- **What it was for** — the brief, the event, the client.

**Store it where you will still have it in two years:**

- Not only on your phone (phones get lost, stolen, broken).
- A **cloud folder** plus a **second copy** (another account or a drive).
- Name files clearly ("2026-03_adire-wrapper_front.jpg").

Choose **quality over quantity**: three excellent, well-documented pieces beat twenty weak ones. Update it as you improve.

## Key words

- **Portfolio:** a documented collection of your best work
- **Caption:** text describing what a piece is and your role
- **Backup:** a second copy kept somewhere else

lessons.summary: What creative people actually get paid for, and how to ask.

## What to do

- Cost one piece: materials, time, travel, revisions
- Practise saying the price out loud without apologising
- List the real income routes in your field: commissions, teaching, performance, licensing

## Understand it

Many creative people find it hard to talk about money — so they undercharge, burn out and give up. Treating creative work as **real work** is how it becomes a living.

**Costing a piece:**

- **Materials** — everything used up.
- **Time** — all of it: planning, making, rehearsing, travel, meetings, admin, **revisions**. Multiply by a fair hourly rate.
- **Travel and equipment** — transport, hire, wear and tear.
- **Revisions** — agree in advance how many are included; more are charged.

**Saying the price:** practise saying it **out loud, plainly, without apologising** — "The fee is ₦80,000." Not "Um, I was thinking maybe around…". Hesitation invites bargaining. If a client cannot afford it, offer a **smaller version**, not a discount on the same work.

**Real income routes** in creative fields — most artists combine several:

- **Commissions** — made-to-order work.
- **Performance fees** — gigs, events, shows.
- **Teaching** — lessons, workshops.
- **Sales** — artworks, merchandise, recordings.
- **Royalties and licensing** — when your work is used or streamed.
- **Grants and prizes** — from arts bodies and foundations.
- **Employment** — studios, theatres, agencies, media companies, churches, schools.

Registering a business name (with the Corporate Affairs Commission in Nigeria) and keeping simple records help when clients and grants want invoices.

## Key words

- **Fee:** the price charged for creative work
- **Revision:** a change requested after delivery
- **Royalty:** payment each time work is used, sold or streamed
- **Income stream:** one source of earnings

lessons.title: Who is it for, and what should they do
lessons.summary: Every piece of media is aimed at somebody and wants something. Decide both before you make anything.
objectives: You will name your audience specifically

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Describe one real person who is your audience — age, place, what they care about
- Write the one thing you want them to do after seeing it
- Discuss: aiming at everyone reaches nobody

## Understand it

Every piece of media — a video, a poster, a post, an article — should start from two decisions:

1. **Who is it for?** Not "everyone" or "young people" but **one real person**: "Amaka, 15, in Surulere, who loves football and is bored at weekends, and checks TikTok every evening." The more specific the person, the clearer every later choice becomes — language, length, format, platform, images.
2. **What should they do after seeing it?** A **desired action** — sign up for the club, come to the event on Saturday, share it with a friend, change a habit, donate. Not just "know about us".

**Why "aiming at everyone reaches nobody":** content that tries to appeal to everyone becomes bland — no one feels it speaks to them. Specific content feels personal, and people share things that feel personal.

Marketers call the imagined person an **audience persona**. Build yours from **real evidence** where you can: talk to people like them, look at what they actually watch and share, ask what they care about.

Test every later decision against the two answers:

- Would *this person* stop scrolling for this?
- Does it make *this action* easy and obvious?

If the answer is no, change it — however much you like it.

## Key words

- **Audience persona:** a specific, realistic description of who the content is for
- **Desired action:** what you want the audience to do after seeing it
- **Call to action:** the clear instruction that prompts the action

lessons.title: The story spine
lessons.summary: The shape underneath anything that holds attention.
objectives: You will write a story spine in five sentences
You will identify the turn
You will say why a list is not a story
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Write it: who, what they want, what is in the way, what they do, what changes
- Mark the turn — the moment it could go either way
- Compare with a piece that is just a list of facts

## Understand it

Facts inform; **stories move** — and people remember and share stories far more than facts. Almost every effective story follows a simple **spine**:

1. **Who** — a character the audience can care about (a real person, a child, a trader, you).
2. **What they want** — a goal.
3. **What is in the way** — an obstacle, a problem, a conflict.
4. **What they do** — the struggle, the attempts.
5. **What changes** — the result, and how the character or situation is different.

Inside it is **the turn** — the moment it could go either way, when the outcome is uncertain. That uncertainty is what keeps an audience watching.

Pixar's storytellers teach a version of this as a fill-in-the-blanks: *Once upon a time… Every day… One day… Because of that… Because of that… Until finally…*

**Compare** two versions of the same content:

- **List of facts:** "Our club has 200 members. We teach coding, music and art. Sessions are on Saturdays."
- **Story:** "Tobi had never touched a computer. Last March she came to her first Saturday session, unsure. Eight weeks later, she showed her mother a website she had built — with her mother's shop on it."

The second makes you **feel** something — and remember it. The facts can still go in, at the end.

## Key words

- **Story spine:** the basic structure: who, want, obstacle, action, change
- **The turn:** the moment the outcome could go either way
- **Character:** the person the audience follows and cares about

lessons.title: Composition
lessons.summary: Where you put things in the frame, which applies to a photo, a video and a page alike.
objectives: You will compose a frame deliberately
You will use leading lines or thirds on purpose
You will say what your frame leaves out
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Shoot or lay out the same subject three ways
- Use the rule of thirds, then break it on purpose
- Name what you excluded — that decision is half of composition

## Understand it

**Composition** is how the elements inside a frame — photo, video shot or layout — are arranged. It controls where the eye goes and what the picture means.

**The rule of thirds:** imagine the frame divided by two horizontal and two vertical lines into nine equal parts. Placing the subject on a line or at a crossing point (rather than dead centre) often creates a more balanced, dynamic image. A horizon on the lower third gives sky; on the upper third, ground. Most phone cameras can show this grid.

**Then break it on purpose.** Centred, symmetrical framing gives power and formality (a portrait looking straight at camera, a building's front). Breaking a rule is fine — **when it is a choice**.

**Other tools:**

- **Leading lines** — roads, rails, edges, shadows that lead the eye to the subject.
- **Framing** — a doorway, window or branches around the subject.
- **Space** — leave room in front of a face or moving subject ("looking room").
- **Angle** — shooting from below makes a subject powerful; from above, smaller or vulnerable.
- **Simplify** — fewer elements, stronger image.

**What you leave out is half of composition.** Every frame **excludes** everything around it. Moving one step left might remove a rubbish heap or a stranger's face. Check the edges and the background before you shoot.

## Key words

- **Composition:** the arrangement of elements in a frame
- **Rule of thirds:** placing subjects on a 3×3 grid's lines or crossings
- **Leading lines:** lines that guide the eye to the subject
- **Framing:** using elements in the scene to surround the subject

lessons.summary: The single biggest difference between amateur and professional work, and it is free.
objectives: You will shoot the same subject in three lighting conditions
You will use a window as a light source
You will say why midday sun is difficult
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Shoot the same face by a window, in shade, and in midday sun
- Use a white surface to bounce light back
- Compare the three honestly

## Understand it

**Light** makes or ruins an image more than the camera does. A cheap phone in good light beats an expensive camera in bad light.

**Three common light situations — compare them on the same face:**

- **Window light** — soft, directional light from one side. Flattering: it shapes the face gently, with soft shadows. The best free light there is. Have the subject face or angle towards the window; never put the window behind them (they become a silhouette).
- **Open shade** — outdoors, but out of direct sun (under a tree, beside a building). Soft and even, with no harsh shadows. Excellent for portraits.
- **Midday sun** — hard, from overhead. Harsh shadows under the eyes, nose and chin; squinting subjects; blown-out (pure white) highlights. Avoid for faces, or move into shade.

**Quality of light:**

- **Hard light** — small or distant source (bare sun, a bare bulb): sharp shadows, high contrast.
- **Soft light** — large source relative to the subject (window, cloudy sky, light bounced off a wall): gentle shadows.

**Bounce:** a **white surface** — a sheet of paper, a white wall, a reflector — placed opposite the light bounces light back into the shadows, softening them. Free and very effective.

**Golden hour** — the hour after sunrise and before sunset — gives warm, soft, low light that photographers love.

Tap on the face on your phone screen to set focus and exposure there.

## Key words

- **Soft light:** light from a large source giving gentle shadows
- **Hard light:** light from a small source giving sharp shadows
- **Bounce:** reflecting light into shadows with a light surface
- **Golden hour:** the warm low light just after sunrise and before sunset

lessons.summary: Audiences forgive bad pictures and leave over bad sound.
objectives: You will record clean audio with what you have
You will get the microphone close
You will say why room noise cannot be removed later
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Record the same line from three distances
- Record in a soft small space and a hard empty one
- Learn: get the mic close, kill the room, check with headphones

## Understand it

Audiences forgive average pictures, but they click away from bad sound within seconds. **Sound is half of video** — and it is the half beginners neglect.

**The three rules:**

1. **Get the mic close.** The single biggest improvement. Sound weakens quickly with distance, while room noise and echo do not. A phone held 20 cm from the speaker's mouth sounds far better than an expensive camera mic three metres away. Use a **lapel (lavalier) mic** if you have one — even a cheap one transforms interviews.
2. **Kill the room.** Hard, bare walls and floors bounce sound, creating **echo** (reverberation) that makes voices sound distant and hollow. Record in **small, soft spaces** — a room with curtains, cushions, carpet, clothes, a car. Avoid large empty halls and tiled rooms.
3. **Check with headphones.** Listen while recording if possible, and always play back before you leave. Problems you do not hear on location — a generator, wind, a buzzing fan, rustling clothes — cannot be fixed later.

**Also:**

- **Turn off** fans and air conditioners while recording; ask people nearby for quiet.
- **Wind** — shield the mic (a foam cover, your body, a sock in an emergency).
- **Record 30 seconds of "room tone"** — silence in the space — useful in editing.
- **Levels** — loud enough, never so loud that it distorts.

## Key words

- **Reverberation (echo):** sound bouncing off hard surfaces
- **Lavalier mic:** a small clip-on microphone
- **Room tone:** a recording of the room's silence, used in editing
- **Distortion:** crackling from recording too loud

lessons.title: Words that carry
lessons.summary: Writing for the ear and the scroll: short, concrete, specific.
objectives: You will cut a paragraph by half without losing meaning
You will replace abstract words with concrete ones
You will read your copy aloud
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Write 100 words, then cut to 50
- Replace every vague word with something you could photograph
- Read it aloud — if you stumble, rewrite it

## Understand it

On screens, people **scan** rather than read — research by the Nielsen Norman Group has shown for years that most web readers skim, catching headings, first words and highlighted items. Writing for media means writing to be **understood in a glance** and remembered after.

**Cut ruthlessly.** Write 100 words, then cut to 50. Most first drafts are padded with throat-clearing ("In today's world…"), repetition, and words like *very, really, basically, actually*. What remains is stronger.

**Be concrete.** Replace every vague word with **something you could photograph**:

- Vague: "Our programme has a positive impact on young people."
- Concrete: "Last term, 40 children built their first website."

Concrete words create pictures in the mind; abstract words slide off.

**Put the most important thing first** (the **inverted pyramid**, from journalism): the key message in the first line, details after. Many people will read only the first line.

**Read it aloud.** If you stumble, the reader will too — rewrite until it flows. Read-aloud catches long sentences, missing words and clumsy rhythm.

**Plain language:** short sentences, common words, active voice ("We opened a centre" not "A centre was opened by us"). Plain writing is not dumbed down — it respects the reader's time.

## Key words

- **Concrete language:** specific words that create pictures
- **Inverted pyramid:** most important information first
- **Plain language:** clear, short, everyday writing
- **Active voice:** the subject does the action

objectives: You will rewrite your earlier story spine

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Reread your week 2 spine
- Rewrite it with a sharper turn and a clearer audience
- Cut one element you were attached to

## Understand it

Rewriting is where good work is made. Professional writers, screenwriters and journalists expect several drafts; the first is just raw material.

**Reread your week 2 spine** with five weeks' more knowledge — and with fresh eyes.

**Sharpen the turn.** Is there a real moment when the outcome is uncertain? If the story goes smoothly from problem to solution, it has no tension. Make the obstacle harder, the stakes clearer, the moment of doubt longer.

**Sharpen the audience.** Does the story speak to your week 1 person? Would *they* recognise themselves, care about the character, understand every word? Adjust the details and language for them.

**Cut one element you were attached to.** Writers call this "killing your darlings": the clever line, the extra scene, the beautiful shot that does not serve the story. If it does not move the story or affect the audience, it goes — however much you like it. The piece gets stronger, and you learn to judge by the work, not by your feelings about it.

**After a night away**, rewrite once more. Distance reveals problems you could not see while writing.

Keep **every version**. Comparing drafts teaches you what rewriting actually changes — and shows how much better work becomes when you go back to it.

## Key words

- **Draft:** one version of a piece of writing
- **Kill your darlings:** cutting favourite parts that do not serve the work

lessons.title: Consent, truth, and what you may publish
lessons.summary: Permission to film someone, honesty about what you changed, and the law.
objectives: You will get and record consent before filming a person
You will say what you must disclose
You will name what you may never publish
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Practise asking permission and recording that you got it
- Learn what must be disclosed: paid promotion, staging, AI-generated or altered content
- Learn what is never published: a child without a guardian's consent, someone's private details, a person in distress

## Understand it

Media has power — to inform, to persuade, and to harm. Professional media makers follow rules about **consent**, **truth** and **what must never be published**.

**Consent:**

- **Ask before** you photograph or film someone identifiable, and explain where it will appear.
- For **children**, you need a **parent or guardian's consent** — and the child's own agreement too.
- **Record** that you got it: a signed release form, a recorded "yes" with name, date and use.
- People can **withdraw** consent; respect it.

**Truth and disclosure:**

- **Paid promotion** must be labelled — "ad", "sponsored", "paid partnership". Hiding it misleads the audience.
- **Staged** scenes presented as real must be disclosed.
- **Generated or heavily altered images and video** must be labelled as such.
- **Check facts** before publishing; correct mistakes openly when you find them.

**What is never published:**

- A **child's full name with their school or location**, or anything that lets a stranger find them.
- **Private information** — addresses, phone numbers, medical details, ID numbers.
- Images of people in **distress or vulnerability** without strong reason and consent.
- Anything that **humiliates** someone.

Nigeria's **Data Protection Act (2023)**, enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, makes personal data a legal responsibility. Organisations like UNICEF publish guidelines on reporting about children ethically.

## Key words

- **Consent:** permission freely given, with understanding of the use
- **Release form:** a signed record of consent to use someone's image
- **Disclosure:** openly stating paid, staged or altered content
- **Personal data:** information that identifies a person

lessons.title: Platforms and formats
lessons.summary: The same story cut three ways, because the platform changes the piece.
objectives: You will adapt one piece for two platforms
You will change the opening for a scrolling audience

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Cut one story as a vertical short and as a longer landscape piece
- Rebuild the first three seconds for a scroll
- Compare what each format forced you to drop

## Understand it

The same story must be **re-cut** for each platform, because each platform is watched differently.

**Vertical short** (TikTok, Reels, Shorts, WhatsApp Status — 9:16):

- Watched on phones, in a scrolling feed, often **without sound**.
- **The first 1–3 seconds decide everything** — start with movement, a face, a question or the most striking moment. No slow logos or introductions.
- **Captions** on screen — many watch muted.
- **Short** — 15–60 seconds; one idea.
- Subjects framed in the centre (edges get covered by buttons and text).

**Longer landscape** (YouTube, websites, presentations — 16:9):

- Watched with intent, often with sound, on bigger screens.
- Room for **context, interviews, b-roll** and a fuller story arc.
- A strong opening still matters, but people give it a little longer.

**What each format forces you to drop:** the short forces you to find the **single strongest moment** and lose the context; the long lets you keep nuance but demands that every section earns its time.

**Write captions for everyone:** captions also help deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers, people in noisy places, and people watching in a second language. Accurate captions are part of accessible media, not an extra.

## Key words

- **Aspect ratio:** the shape of the frame — 9:16 vertical, 16:9 landscape
- **Hook:** the opening seconds that stop the scroll
- **Captions:** on-screen text of what is said
- **B-roll:** supporting footage cut over speech

lessons.title: Did it work?
lessons.summary: Choosing the measure before publishing, and ignoring the flattering one.
objectives: You will choose one success measure before publishing
You will record the result honestly
You will name a vanity metric
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Pick the one number that matches your week 1 desired action
- Publish, wait, and record the result
- Spot the vanity metrics: views, likes, follows

## Understand it

"Did it work?" can only be answered against the goal you set in week 1 — the **desired action**. Measure that, not whatever number is biggest.

**Pick the one number that matches the action:**

- Goal: sign-ups → count **sign-ups** (form submissions), not views.
- Goal: event attendance → count **people who came**.
- Goal: donations → count **donations** and amount.
- Goal: awareness among parents in one area → a short **survey**, or questions at the next event: "How did you hear about us?"

**Vanity metrics** — numbers that look impressive but tell you little about whether the content achieved anything:

- **Views** — a view may be one second of a scroll.
- **Likes** — easy to give, rarely mean action.
- **Follower count** — can be bought, and many followers never see your posts.

They are not useless — reach matters — but they **flatter** more than they inform. The Nielsen Norman Group describes vanity metrics as numbers that need context to mean anything.

**Measure honestly:**

- **Decide the measure before you publish** — otherwise you will be tempted to pick whichever number looks best afterwards.
- **Wait** a fixed period (a week).
- **Record** the result, even when disappointing.
- **Compare** with something — a previous post, a different version.

An honest small result teaches more than an impressive meaningless one.

## Key words

- **Metric:** a number used to measure results
- **Vanity metric:** a number that looks good but shows little real effect
- **Conversion:** someone taking the desired action

lessons.summary: Someone else is paying, and revisions are part of the job.
objectives: You will take a brief and confirm it in writing
You will agree how many revisions are included
You will handle one revision request professionally
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Take a brief and write back what you understood — this prevents most disputes
- Agree the number of revisions and what counts as a new job
- Take a revision without arguing, and deliver it

## Understand it

Working for a client is where media skills become income — and where most problems come from **misunderstanding**, not poor work.

**Write back what you understood.** After receiving a brief, send the client a short summary in your own words: the audience, the desired action, the format, the length, the deadline, the budget, what they will provide (logos, photos, access). Ask them to confirm. This one step **prevents most disputes** — misunderstandings surface before work starts, not after.

**Agree on revisions in advance:**

- **How many** rounds of changes are included (often two).
- **What counts as a revision** (changes to what was agreed — a different photo, shorter text, a colour change) and what counts as **a new job** (a completely different concept, a new format, extra deliverables) — charged separately.
- **Deadlines** for feedback, so a project does not drag on for months.

**Taking feedback professionally:**

- Do not argue or take it personally. Ask questions to understand the **reason** behind a change ("Is the concern that the text is hard to read?").
- If you think a change will harm the result, say so **once**, briefly, with your reason — then do what the client decides. It is their project.
- **Deliver on time**, as agreed.

Put agreements **in writing** — even a WhatsApp message or email counts as a record.

## Key words

- **Brief:** the client's description of what they need
- **Revision round:** one set of changes after the client's review
- **Scope:** what is included in the agreed job
- **Scope creep:** extra work added without extra payment

## What to do

- Publish your finished piece
- Present the audience, the desired action, the measure and the result
- Say what you would do differently and why

## Understand it

Publishing — sending your work out to a real audience — is the test of everything in the course.

**Before publishing, check:**

- **Consent** for every identifiable person, especially children (week 8).
- **Facts** — names, dates, numbers spelled and stated correctly.
- **Rights** — music, images and footage you own or are licensed to use.
- **Captions** and accessibility.
- **Disclosures** — paid, staged or altered content labelled.
- **The call to action** — clear and easy to follow.

**Present it as a strategist would:**

1. **The audience** — your specific person.
2. **The desired action**.
3. **The measure** — the one number, chosen in advance.
4. **The result** — honestly reported, after the waiting period.

**Say what you would do differently, and why.** This is the most valuable part. "I would put the hook in the first second, because most viewers dropped off at 3 seconds" is real learning; "it went well" is not.

The cycle you have learnt — **audience → action → story → craft → ethics → format → measure → improve** — is how media professionals work, from small businesses to large agencies. Every piece you publish is a small experiment; each one should make the next one better.

## Key words

- **Publishing:** releasing work to a real audience
- **Pre-publish checklist:** the checks made before anything goes out
- **Iteration:** improving with each new attempt based on results

lessons.title: Computational thinking
lessons.summary: Breaking a problem down, finding the pattern, ignoring the detail, writing the steps.
objectives: You will decompose a real task into steps
You will find the repeating pattern in it
You will write it as an algorithm somebody else can follow
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Take a real task — making tea, marking a register — and decompose it
- Find what repeats
- Write the steps precisely enough for a classmate to follow exactly

## Understand it

**Computational thinking** is the way engineers and programmers approach problems — and it works on problems that have nothing to do with computers. It has four parts:

1. **Decomposition** — breaking a big problem into smaller ones. "Run a registration desk" becomes: greet, find the name, check payment, give a badge, record attendance.
2. **Pattern recognition** — noticing what repeats. Every person at the desk goes through the same steps; only the name changes. Repeated steps can be written once and reused (a **loop**).
3. **Abstraction** — ignoring details that do not matter. To mark a register, the colour of someone's shirt is irrelevant; their name and status are not.
4. **Algorithms** — writing a precise, step-by-step solution that anyone (or any machine) can follow and get the same result.

**The precision test:** write the steps for making tea so exactly that a classmate can follow them **literally**, doing nothing you did not write. Most first attempts fail — "boil water" (in what? how much? how do I know it's boiling?), "add sugar" (how much? when?). Computers are the ultimate literal followers: they do exactly what you say, not what you mean.

Good algorithms also handle **decisions** ("if there is no milk, then…") and **ending conditions** ("stop when the cup is three-quarters full").

This is the foundation of programming, engineering and good process design in business.

## Key words

- **Decomposition:** breaking a problem into smaller parts
- **Pattern recognition:** spotting what repeats
- **Abstraction:** keeping only the details that matter
- **Algorithm:** a precise sequence of steps that solves a problem

## Read and watch

- [What is computational thinking?](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/guides/zp92mp3/revision/1) — BBC Bitesize
- [Computational thinking (KS3)](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/topics/z7tp34j) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Decompose a second task and have someone follow it
1. Fix every step they got stuck on

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Do it on paper first. If you cannot describe the steps, the computer cannot do them for you either.
- **If you already can:** Make it fail on purpose, handle the failure, and write the test that proves it is handled.

lessons.summary: What data actually is, where it lives, and what shape it should be in.
objectives: You will put messy data into a consistent shape
You will name the fields and their types
You will say why inconsistent data cannot be counted
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Take a messy list and give it consistent columns
- Name each field and what kind of value it holds
- Try to count something in the messy version and feel why it fails

## Understand it

Almost every technology system runs on **data** — and badly structured data is behind many software failures and business mistakes.

**Messy data** looks like a list written by many hands:

- "Tobi, 14, Surulere" / "ADEBAYO Tunde - 13yrs" / "Chidinma (12) Yaba" / "tobi 14 surulere"

Try to **count** how many are 14, or how many from Surulere, and you have to read each one by eye. Duplicates hide ("Tobi" and "tobi"). Errors go unnoticed.

**Structured data** puts each fact in its own **column (field)** with a consistent **type**:

| firstName | surname | age | area |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tobi | — | 14 | Surulere |
| Tunde | Adebayo | 13 | — |

Now a computer (or a spreadsheet filter) can count, sort, search and spot duplicates instantly.

**Designing a field:**

- **Name** it clearly ("dateOfBirth", not "info").
- Decide its **type**: text, whole number, date, yes/no, one choice from a list.
- Decide what is **allowed**: an age between 5 and 25; an area from a fixed list (prevents "Surulere" vs "surulere" vs "Surulere ").
- Decide whether it is **required**.

**One fact, one place:** store a date of birth, not an age (which goes out of date). Store first name and surname separately if you will ever sort by surname.

Spreadsheets enforce this with **data validation**; databases enforce it with **schemas**.

## Key words

- **Field (column):** one kind of fact in a table
- **Record (row):** all the fields for one item
- **Data type:** the kind of value a field holds — text, number, date
- **Validation:** rules that reject bad values

## Read and watch

lessons.title: Systems
lessons.summary: Input, process, output, feedback — in software, in a robot, and in a queue at the gate.
objectives: You will draw a system diagram for something real
You will identify its feedback loop
You will find where it would fail
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Draw a real system: the check-in desk, a traffic light, a bank app
- Mark the feedback — what tells the system how it is doing
- Mark the point where it breaks if one part is slow

## Understand it

A **system** is a set of parts that work together to achieve something — a check-in desk, a traffic light junction, a bank app, a water supply, a school timetable. Engineers draw systems to understand them, improve them, and predict where they will fail.

**Drawing a system:**

- **Inputs** — what comes in (people, requests, money, data, electricity).
- **Processes** — what happens to them (checked, stored, approved, transformed).
- **Outputs** — what comes out (a badge, a payment, a green light).
- **Arrows** — how things flow between parts.

**Feedback** — information about how the system is doing, which comes back and changes what it does:

- A thermostat measures temperature and switches the AC on or off.
- A queue that grows tells the desk manager to open a second desk.
- A banking app shows a failed payment, so the user tries again.

Systems without feedback cannot correct themselves.

**Bottlenecks** — the slowest part limits the whole system. If the check-in desk can register 3 people a minute but the badge printer manages 1, the queue grows at the printer, however fast the desk is. Speeding up anything else does nothing; fix the bottleneck.

**Failure points** — ask of each part: *what happens if this is slow? If it stops? If it receives bad input?* A good system design has a plan — a backup, a manual process, a clear error message — for each.

You will use this thinking in software, electronics, business processes and project planning.

## Key words

- **System:** parts working together to achieve a purpose
- **Feedback loop:** information about results that changes what the system does
- **Bottleneck:** the slowest part, which limits the whole system
- **Failure point:** a part whose failure affects the system

lessons.title: Debugging anything
lessons.summary: Reproduce, isolate, fix, verify — the method, applied to code and to a broken fan alike.
objectives: You will reproduce a fault reliably before changing anything
You will halve the search space to isolate it
You will verify the fix against the original symptom
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Reproduce the fault on demand first
- Halve the possibilities repeatedly until you find it
- Fix one thing, then verify against the original steps

## Understand it

**Debugging** — finding and fixing faults — is most of an engineer's working life. The good news is that it is a **method**, not a talent.

**1. Reproduce it on demand.** Before fixing anything, find exact steps that make the fault happen **every time**. "It sometimes crashes" cannot be fixed; "it crashes when I submit the form with an empty name field" can. If you cannot make it happen, you cannot prove you fixed it.

**2. Read the evidence.** Error messages, logs, what you see. Read error messages **fully** — they often say exactly what and where.

**3. Halve the possibilities.** This is **binary search**, and it is very powerful. If a program has 100 steps and the result is wrong at the end, check step 50: is the value right there? If yes, the fault is in 51–100; if no, in 1–50. Check the middle of the half. In about 7 checks you have found the step — out of 100. Works for code, circuits, and long processes alike.

**4. Form a hypothesis**, then test it. "I think the name is empty because the form field has the wrong id" — check that, specifically.

**5. Change one thing at a time.** Change three things at once and it works — which one fixed it? Change one and it breaks something else — you know why.

**6. Verify** against the original steps from (1). The fault should be gone, and nothing else broken.

**7. Write down** what it was and how you found it. You will meet it again.

## Key words

- **Bug:** a fault that makes something behave wrongly
- **Reproduce:** make a fault happen reliably, on demand
- **Binary search:** halving the possibilities each step
- **Hypothesis:** a specific, testable guess at the cause

## Read and watch

lessons.title: Evidence
lessons.summary: Testing: proving something works rather than believing it does.
objectives: You will write a test that would catch a real failure
You will test an edge case
You will say why "it worked when I tried it" is not evidence
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Write a check that fails when the thing is broken
- Test the edges: empty, zero, very large, missing, duplicated
- Discuss: one successful try is an anecdote

## Understand it

"It works — I tried it" is the most dangerous sentence in engineering. **One successful try is an anecdote, not evidence.** Something can work once and fail on the next input, the next day, or for the next user.

**A test is a check that fails when the thing is broken.** If the test cannot fail, it proves nothing. Write it so that you can deliberately break the thing and watch the test go red.

**Test the edges**, because that is where faults hide:

- **Empty** — no name, an empty list, a blank form.
- **Zero** — zero quantity, zero price, division by zero.
- **Very large** — a 500-character name, 10,000 records, a huge file.
- **Missing** — no internet, a missing file, a deleted record.
- **Duplicated** — the same person registered twice; the button pressed twice.
- **Wrong type** — letters in a number field; a date in the wrong format.
- **Boundaries** — if ages 5 to 25 are allowed, test 4, 5, 25 and 26.

**Automated tests** — code that tests code — run in seconds every time something changes, catching faults before users do. Frameworks such as **Jest** (JavaScript) and **pytest** (Python) make them easy to write.

For physical things, the same idea holds: a bridge design is tested at loads beyond normal use; a circuit is tested at its limits.

The engineer's question is not "does it work?" but "**how would I know if it didn't?**"

## Key words

- **Test:** a check that fails when something is broken
- **Edge case:** an extreme or unusual input
- **Boundary value:** a value at the edge of what is allowed
- **Automated test:** code that checks other code automatically

## Read and watch

lessons.title: Safe by default
lessons.summary: Security and privacy as a design decision, not a step at the end.
objectives: You will list what data your project holds
You will remove what you do not need
You will say why collecting less is safer
lessons.body:
## What to do

- List every piece of data your project touches
- Delete every field you do not actually need
- Learn the rule: data you never collected cannot leak

## Understand it

Every piece of personal data a system holds is a **responsibility** — and a risk. Data can be **leaked** (hacked, a laptop lost, a spreadsheet emailed to the wrong person), **misused**, or **kept longer than it should be**.

**The simplest security rule: data you never collected cannot leak.** This principle is called **data minimisation**, and it is part of data protection laws worldwide, including Nigeria's **Data Protection Act 2023**.

**Audit your project's data:**

1. **List every field** your project collects or stores.
2. For each, ask: **what do we actually use it for?** If the answer is "it might be useful" — delete it.
3. Ask whether you can use **less sensitive** data: an age range instead of a date of birth; a town instead of a full address.
4. Decide **how long** you keep it, and delete it after.
5. Decide **who can see it** — only those who need it.

**Safe by default** means the safest setting is the starting setting:

- New accounts are **private** until the user chooses otherwise.
- Access is **refused** unless specifically granted (least privilege).
- Passwords are **hashed**, never stored as plain text.
- Sensitive data is **encrypted**.
- Forms collect the **minimum**.

Think especially about **children's data**: names with schools and locations, photos and contact details need the strongest protection.

## Key words

- **Data minimisation:** collecting only the data you actually need
- **Least privilege:** giving each person only the access they need
- **Safe by default:** the safest settings are the starting settings
- **Encryption:** scrambling data so only authorised people can read it

## Read and watch

- [Small organisations guide to cyber security](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/small-business-guide) — UK National Cyber Security Centre

lessons.summary: Returning to the week 4 method and applying it to a physical fault.
objectives: You will apply the debugging method to a physical object
You will prove the cause before replacing anything
You will say what transfers between the two
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Find a physical fault — a torch, a fan, a cable — and work the method
- Prove the cause by swapping one thing at a time
- Compare with how you debugged code in week 4

## Understand it

The debugging method from week 4 is not only for software. It works on a torch, a fan, a phone charger, a generator, a bicycle — anything with parts.

**The same steps, on a physical fault:**

1. **Reproduce** — when exactly does it fail? Always? Only when cold? Only when moved?
2. **Gather evidence** — look, listen, smell (burning?), feel (hot?), measure (a **multimeter** measures voltage, current and continuity).
3. **Halve the possibilities** — split the system: is power reaching the device? (Yes → the fault is inside. No → the fault is in the supply or cable.) Then halve again.
4. **Hypothesis** — "I think the battery contact is corroded."
5. **Swap one thing at a time** — a known-good battery, a known-good cable, a known-good bulb. Each swap tests one hypothesis. Swapping two things at once leaves you not knowing which was faulty.
6. **Verify** — the original failure no longer happens.

**Safety first with physical things:**

- **Unplug** before opening anything mains-powered. Mains electricity can kill.
- Never open **microwaves, TVs with tubes, or power supplies** — capacitors store dangerous charge even when unplugged.
- **Batteries** — do not short-circuit, puncture or heat lithium batteries; they can catch fire.

**Compare with week 4:** what was the same? (The method.) What was different? (The evidence — a multimeter instead of an error message — and the safety.)

## Key words

- **Multimeter:** a meter that measures voltage, current and resistance
- **Continuity:** whether a circuit is complete
- **Known-good part:** a part you know works, used for comparison

## What to do

- Use it to explain an error or review a design, then check it
- Find one confident wrong answer and record it
- Agree: the person who ships it is responsible, not the tool

## Understand it

AI assistants are now part of engineering work — explaining errors, suggesting code, reviewing designs, drafting documentation. Used well, they speed up learning and work. Used carelessly, they produce **confident wrong answers** that look exactly like right ones.

**Where they help:**

- **Explaining an error message** in plain language.
- **Explaining unfamiliar code** line by line.
- **Suggesting approaches** you had not considered.
- **Reviewing** a design or code for issues you missed.
- **Drafting** boilerplate and documentation for you to edit.

**Where they go wrong:**

- **Invented details** — functions, settings, library features or references that do not exist (often called "hallucinations").
- **Outdated information** — APIs and best practices change.
- **Plausible but subtly wrong** code — works on the example, fails on edge cases; insecure patterns.
- **Missing context** — they do not know your system, your users or your constraints.

**Working honestly with them:**

1. **Check everything** — run the code, test the edges (week 5), look up the documentation.
2. **Understand before you use** — if you cannot explain the code, do not ship it.
3. **Never paste secrets** (passwords, keys) or **personal data** into an assistant.
4. **Record** a confident wrong answer when you find one — it trains your judgement.

**The person who ships it is responsible, not the tool.** If an engineer deploys code that leaks data, "the assistant wrote it" is no defence.

## Key words

- **Hallucination:** a confident, plausible but false output from an AI model
- **Verification:** checking a result independently
- **Accountability:** being responsible for what you ship

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Write: what it is, how to run it, what breaks it, who to ask
- Give it to a classmate and watch without helping
- Fix every place they stopped

## Understand it

A project that only its maker can run is fragile: when they are ill, busy or gone, it stops. **Documentation** lets someone else use, run, fix and improve it.

**The four things every project's documentation needs (usually a README file):**

1. **What it is** — one or two sentences: what it does and for whom.
2. **How to run it** — exact steps from a fresh start: what to install, which commands, which settings. Assume the reader knows nothing about your setup.
3. **What breaks it** — known limitations, common errors and their fixes, what it does not do.
4. **Who to ask** — the owner, and where to report problems.

Useful extras: a screenshot, an example, how to run the tests, the licence.

**The usability test for documentation:** give it to a classmate who has never seen the project, and **watch without helping**. Every place they stop, hesitate, or ask a question is a gap. **Fix every one.** (Engineers are often shocked how many steps they left out because they "just knew".)

**Write it while you build**, not at the end — you remember the details, and the documentation helps you too.

**Keep it current**: wrong documentation is worse than none, because people trust it.

This is the same principle as the organisation's own standard: a process or system must work without its creator.

## Key words

- **README:** the main documentation file of a project
- **Setup instructions:** exact steps to get something running from scratch
- **Known issues:** documented limitations and problems

## What to do

- Put a project under version control and commit with real messages
- Write an issue: what happens, what should happen, how to reproduce
- Review a classmate's work with two specific comments

## Understand it

Real engineering is a team activity, and teams use shared tools and habits so that many people can work on one project without chaos.

**Version control (Git)** records every change to a project:

- Each saved change is a **commit**, with a **message** saying what changed and why.
- You can see the **history**, compare versions, and **undo** mistakes.
- **Branches** let people work on different things in parallel, then **merge** them.
- Services like **GitHub** host projects online so teams can share them.

**Good commit messages** — short summary first ("Fix crash when name is empty"), then why if needed. "Update" or "stuff" tells no one anything.

**Issues** — the team's list of problems and tasks. A good bug report says:

1. **What happens** (the actual behaviour).
2. **What should happen** (the expected behaviour).
3. **How to reproduce it** — exact steps.
4. Device, browser or version; screenshots.

**Code review** — before changes are merged, a teammate reviews them. Good reviews are **specific**:

- Not "looks good" or "this is bad", but "line 42: this fails if the list is empty — add a check?"
- Comment on the **code**, not the person.
- Mention one thing done well as well as what to improve.

Review catches bugs early and spreads knowledge across the team.

## Key words

- **Version control:** a system recording every change to files
- **Commit:** a saved change with a message
- **Issue:** a recorded problem or task
- **Code review:** teammates checking changes before they are merged

## What to do

- List everyone affected, including people who never use it
- Name the most likely harm, honestly
- Change one design decision to reduce it

## Understand it

Every technology affects people — including many who **never use it**. Engineers who think only about their users miss harms that land on others.

**List everyone affected:**

- **Users** — the people who use it directly.
- **People the data is about** — a school attendance system affects children who never log in.
- **People nearby** — a generator's noise and fumes affect neighbours; a camera records passers-by.
- **People left out** — those without smartphones, data, literacy, or who have a disability.
- **Workers** — whose jobs change because of it.
- **The environment** — energy, e-waste.

**Name the most likely harm, honestly.** Not the most dramatic one — the **most likely**. For a club attendance app: a child's location and schedule exposed; parents without smartphones unable to see updates; a mistaken "absent" mark leading to a wrong accusation.

**Change one design decision to reduce it:**

- Hide locations from public view.
- Offer an SMS option.
- Let staff correct mistakes, with a record of who changed what.

**Bias and fairness:** systems trained or designed around one group can fail others — face recognition that works worse on darker skin, forms that do not fit Nigerian names or addresses. Test with the **real range** of people who will be affected.

This is the question behind accessibility standards, data protection law and engineering ethics codes: **who could this hurt, and what have we done about it?**

## Key words

- **Stakeholder:** anyone affected by a system
- **Harm:** damage a system could cause to people
- **Accessibility:** designing so people with disabilities can use it
- **Bias:** a system working better for some groups than others

## What to do

- Demonstrate your build working
- Show the tests passing and one failure mode you handled
- Defend three decisions, including one thing you deliberately left out

## Understand it

"Build and defend" is how engineering work is judged in industry — at design reviews, client demos and job interviews. You show it working, prove it is reliable, and explain your decisions.

**1. Demonstrate it working** — the real thing, on real inputs, not a slideshow. Prepare the demo: data ready, steps rehearsed, a backup (screenshots or a video) in case of a failed connection.

**2. Show the tests passing** (week 5) — and **one failure mode you handled**: "If the internet drops during upload, it saves locally and retries — watch." Showing how it fails safely is more impressive than claiming it never fails.

**3. Defend three decisions:**

- **Why this approach** rather than an alternative.
- **A trade-off** you made (simpler but slower; safer but less convenient).
- **One thing you deliberately left out** — and why. Knowing what *not* to build is a sign of engineering judgement: "I didn't build accounts, because a shared code was enough for 20 users and avoided storing passwords."

**4. Show the documentation** (week 9) and who is affected (week 11).

**Taking questions:**

- Listen to the whole question.
- Answer with **evidence**, not confidence.
- "I don't know — here's how I would find out" is a strong answer. Making something up is a weak one.

Reflect: what would you build next, and what would you change if you started again?

## Key words

- **Demo:** a live demonstration of a working system
- **Trade-off:** gaining one benefit at the cost of another
- **Failure mode:** a way a system can fail, and how it behaves when it does
- **Scope decision:** a deliberate choice of what not to build

lessons.summary: Somebody has a problem, you solve it, they pay more than it cost you.
objectives: You will explain a real business in one sentence

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Pick a real business near you and explain it in one sentence
- Name who pays, what it costs to serve them, what is left
- Learn the difference between money in and money kept

## Understand it

Strip any business — a market stall, a barbershop, a bank, a tech start-up — down to its core, and it does one thing: **it creates something people value enough to pay for, at a cost lower than what they pay**.

Three questions explain almost any business:

1. **Who pays?** (The customer — not always the user: for a free app, advertisers pay; for a school, parents pay.)
2. **What does it cost to serve them?** Ingredients, stock, rent, staff, transport, data, electricity.
3. **What is left?** The **profit** — what the business keeps.

**Money in is not money kept.** This is the most important distinction in business:

- **Revenue (turnover / sales)** — all the money coming in.
- **Profit** — what is left **after all costs**.

A trader who sells ₦500,000 of goods a month sounds successful. If the goods cost ₦420,000 and stall rent, transport and the assistant cost ₦100,000, the business **lost ₦20,000** — despite high sales. Many businesses fail while busy, because the owner watched revenue, not profit.

**Explaining a business in one sentence** ("We sell freshly made zobo to office workers in Ikeja, delivered before lunch") forces clarity: who, what, where, and why they would choose you.

Pick a real business near you. Who pays? What does it cost to serve them? What is left?

## Key words

- **Revenue:** all the money coming into a business
- **Profit:** what remains after all costs are paid
- **Customer:** the person or organisation that pays
- **Business model:** how a business creates value and makes money

lessons.title: Customers, and evidence
lessons.summary: What people say, what they do, and which to believe.
objectives: You will ask about a past behaviour rather than a future intention
You will observe one real transaction
You will say why "would you buy this?" is a weak question
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Interview: ask about the last time they bought, not whether they would
- Watch one real transaction happen
- Compare what you were told with what you saw

## Understand it

The most common reason new products and businesses fail is that **not enough people want them** — and the founders did not find out before spending money. Good businesses decide from **evidence**, not opinion.

**Why "Would you buy this?" is a bad question:** people are polite; they imagine a better version of themselves; saying yes costs nothing. Most will say yes — and never buy.

**Ask about past behaviour instead** — what people **actually did**:

- "When did you last buy snacks at school? What did you buy? How much did you spend?"
- "What do you use now to solve this? What annoys you about it?"
- "How did you find the last tailor you used?"

Past behaviour is the best predictor of future behaviour.

**Watch real transactions.** Stand near a shop, a bus stop or a canteen and **observe**: what do people buy, when, how much do they spend, how long do they wait, what makes them walk away? Observation often contradicts what people say.

**Compare what you were told with what you saw.** The gap is valuable information. Someone who says "I always buy healthy snacks" but buys chin chin every time is telling you something.

**Good interviewing:** listen more than you talk; do not pitch your idea (it biases answers); ask "why?" and "tell me more"; write down their words.

This is the core of **customer research**, used by start-ups, government services and large companies alike.

## Key words

- **Customer research:** finding out what customers actually need and do
- **Past behaviour:** what people actually did — a better guide than what they say
- **Observation:** watching real behaviour directly

lessons.summary: The three numbers, and knowing which one you are looking at.
objectives: You will separate fixed from variable costs
You will calculate margin per unit
You will find the break-even point
lessons.body:
## What to do

- List costs that happen anyway and costs that happen per sale
- Work out what is left on one unit
- Work out how many units cover the fixed costs

## Understand it

Three ideas explain whether a business can survive: **costs, margin and break-even**.

**Two kinds of cost:**

- **Fixed costs** — happen **anyway**, whether you sell nothing or a thousand: rent, salaries, loan repayments, subscriptions, a generator's maintenance.
- **Variable costs** — happen **per sale**: ingredients, packaging, delivery, payment fees. Sell more, spend more.

**Margin per unit** (contribution): what is left on each sale after its variable cost.

- A cup of zobo sells for ₦500. Ingredients, cup and lid cost ₦200. **Margin = ₦300 per cup.**

**Break-even:** how many units must you sell to cover your fixed costs?

- Fixed costs: ₦60,000 a month (stall rent, fridge running, phone).
- Break-even = fixed costs ÷ margin per unit = 60,000 ÷ 300 = **200 cups a month**.
- Sell 200 → no profit, no loss. Sell 300 → profit of 100 × ₦300 = ₦30,000. Sell 150 → loss of ₦15,000.

**What this tells you:**

- Is the break-even number **realistic**? 200 cups a month is about 8 a day — possible. 2,000 a month might not be.
- How to improve: **raise the price**, **cut variable cost**, **cut fixed costs**, or **sell more**.
- Why low prices are dangerous: a small margin needs a huge volume to break even.

Do the same for a real product you know.

## Key words

- **Fixed cost:** a cost that stays the same however much you sell
- **Variable cost:** a cost that rises with each sale
- **Margin (contribution):** price minus variable cost, per unit
- **Break-even point:** the sales needed to cover all fixed costs
