## What to do

- Design the smallest record that answers a real question
- Record a week of real activity in it
- Discuss: a business that lives in one head cannot be handed over, sold or audited

## Understand it

A business whose knowledge lives in **one person's head** cannot be handed over, sold, audited, financed or grown. When that person is ill, travels or leaves, the business stalls. **Records** make a business real.

**Start from a question, not a form.** Design the **smallest record** that answers a real question:

- "How much did we actually make this month?" → a daily sales and expenses log: date, item, amount in, amount out, payment method.
- "Who owes us money?" → a debtors list: name, amount, date, due date, paid?
- "What stock do we have?" → a stock sheet: item, quantity, date counted.
- "Which customers come back?" → a customer list with visit dates.

Record only what answers the question. Records that take too long to keep are abandoned.

**Record a real week** of activity. You will discover problems quickly: missing entries, unclear categories, transactions you forgot.

**Good records are:**

- **Kept daily** — memory fails within days.
- **Consistent** — same categories, same format.
- **Backed up** — a spreadsheet in the cloud beats a notebook that can get wet or lost (keep receipts too).
- **Separate from personal money** — mixing business and personal spending is how owners lose track of whether the business makes a profit.

Records are also what banks, investors, tax authorities and grant givers ask for.

## Key words

- **Record:** a written account of transactions or activity
- **Ledger:** a record of money in and out
- **Debtor:** someone who owes the business money
- **Audit:** an independent check of records

## What to do

- Write a real process as numbered steps
- Mark every point where someone has to decide, and what decides it
- Give it to a classmate and watch them follow it

## Understand it

A **process** is a repeatable way of getting something done: opening the shop, taking an order, onboarding a new member, paying a supplier. Written processes let **anyone** do the job to the same standard — which is how businesses grow beyond their founders.

**Writing a process:**

1. **Name it and its goal**: "Taking a phone order — so every order is recorded correctly and delivered on time."
2. **Numbered steps**, each starting with a verb: "1. Greet the customer and take their name. 2. Write the order on the order sheet…"
3. **Decision points** — mark every place where someone must choose, and **what decides it**: "If the item is out of stock → offer the alternative from the list. If they refuse → note it and end the call politely."
4. **Inputs and outputs** — what is needed to start (order sheet, price list) and what is produced (a completed order record).
5. **Owner** — who is responsible for the process and for keeping it up to date.

**Flowcharts** show the same thing visually: boxes for steps, diamonds for decisions, arrows for flow.

**The test:** give it to a classmate and **watch them follow it**, without helping. Every point where they hesitate, guess, or do something different from what you intended reveals a gap. **Fix every one.**

A process that only works when its author is in the room is not yet a process.

## Key words

- **Process:** a repeatable sequence of steps to achieve a result
- **Decision point:** a step where the path depends on a condition
- **Flowchart:** a diagram of a process with steps and decisions
- **Process owner:** the person responsible for a process

lessons.title: Writing that gets a decision
lessons.summary: The short message that makes a busy person able to say yes or no.
objectives: You will write a request with the ask in the first line
You will give the options and a recommendation
You will keep it under 150 words
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Put the ask first — a busy reader may not reach paragraph three
- Give two or three options and say which you recommend
- Cut to under 150 words

## Understand it

In organisations, decisions are made by busy people who read quickly and may stop after the first few lines. Writing that gets a decision is built for that reader.

**Put the ask first.** The first sentence says what you need: "I need your approval to spend ₦150,000 on a second fridge by Friday." Not three paragraphs of background first — the reader may never reach the request. This is sometimes called **"bottom line up front"**.

**Then give options, and recommend one:**

- **Option A:** buy a second fridge (₦150,000) — doubles cold storage; pays for itself in about 6 weeks from reduced spoilage.
- **Option B:** rent cold-room space (₦20,000/month) — no upfront cost; less convenient.
- **Option C:** do nothing — we continue losing about ₦25,000/month in spoiled stock.
- **I recommend A**, because…

Giving options shows you have thought it through; recommending one shows judgement and saves the reader work.

**Keep it short** — under 150 words for most decisions. Cut background the reader already knows. Use numbers, not adjectives ("₦25,000 a month", not "significant losses").

**End with the specific next step and deadline**: "If you approve by Wednesday, I'll order on Thursday."

The same structure works for emails, WhatsApp messages to a manager, memos and proposals.

## Key words

- **Bottom line up front:** putting the main point or request first
- **Options paper:** a short document comparing choices
- **Recommendation:** the option you advise, with your reason

## Read and watch

- [Inverted pyramid](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/inverted-pyramid/) — Nielsen Norman Group
- [Plain language guidelines](https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/) — plainlanguage.gov

1. Write two more requests in that shape
1. Send one for real and see how fast it is answered

lessons.title: Re-costing with real numbers
lessons.summary: Returning to the week 3 calculation with figures you actually checked.
objectives: You will replace your estimates with real prices
You will compare the two versions
You will say what you had underestimated
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Go to a market or a supplier and get real prices
- Redo the week 3 calculation
- Name what you had got most wrong

## Understand it

In week 3 you estimated costs. Estimates feel right in a classroom — and are usually wrong in the market. Real prices are the only way to know whether the business works.

**Get real prices:**

- Go to a **market** or call **suppliers**. Ask for the price of the actual quantities you would buy.
- Check **at least two sources** — prices vary between markets and sellers.
- Note **bulk discounts**, **transport costs** to fetch goods, and **minimum orders**.
- Note the **date** — in an inflationary economy, prices move monthly.

**Redo the week 3 calculation** with the real numbers: variable cost per unit, margin per unit, fixed costs, break-even.

**Name what you got most wrong.** Common surprises:

- **Packaging** costs far more than expected.
- **Transport** — getting stock to the business and products to customers.
- **Waste** — spoilage, breakage, unsold items.
- **Small costs that add up** — data, phone, POS charges, bank fees.
- **Your own time**, left out entirely.

Did break-even go up? Is the business still realistic?

**Keep re-costing.** Write the date on every costing, and update it regularly. Businesses that set prices once and never check them slowly lose money as costs rise around them.

## Key words

- **Costing:** working out what a product costs to make or supply
- **Estimate:** an approximate figure before real data
- **Inflation:** the general rise in prices over time
- **Bulk discount:** a lower price per unit for larger quantities

lessons.title: Deciding what not to do
lessons.summary: Prioritisation, and saying no so that something can actually be finished.
objectives: You will rank six tasks by value and effort
You will cut the bottom half
You will refuse one request with a reason and an alternative
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Score six real tasks: value against effort
- Draw the line and cut
- Practise refusing: acknowledge, reason, alternative

## Understand it

Strategy is as much about what you **will not** do as what you will. Every business and every person has more possible tasks than time — doing everything means doing everything badly.

**Score tasks: value against effort.** Plot each task on a simple 2×2 grid:

- **High value, low effort** — **quick wins**: do these first.
- **High value, high effort** — **major projects**: plan and schedule them.
- **Low value, low effort** — **fill-ins**: only if there is spare time.
- **Low value, high effort** — **cut these**.

Software teams use similar scoring frameworks (for example **RICE**: reach, impact, confidence, effort) for the same purpose.

**Draw the line and cut.** Decide how many tasks you can actually do well, and drop the rest — deliberately and explicitly. A short list that is finished beats a long list that is half-done.

**Saying no** is a professional skill. A good refusal has three parts:

1. **Acknowledge** — "Thank you, that sounds like a useful event."
2. **Reason** — "We've committed this month to the registration drive, and taking on another project would put that at risk."
3. **Alternative** — "Could we look at it in March? Or I can share the contact of someone who might help."

This keeps relationships good while protecting focus.

Re-rank after a day: first scores are often driven by excitement or anxiety rather than value.

## Key words

- **Prioritisation:** deciding what to do first, and what not at all
- **Value/effort matrix:** a grid comparing a task's benefit with its cost
- **Opportunity cost:** what you give up by choosing one option

## Read and watch

- [Prioritisation frameworks](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/prioritization-framework) — Atlassian

- [How to say no](https://www.mindtools.com/a2az7e1/how-to-say-no) — Mind Tools

## Practise at home

1. Re-rank after a day
1. Practise one refusal aloud
1. **With an AI assistant —** ask it to argue for the task you cut, as strongly as it can, then decide again yourself. If the argument changes your mind, your ranking was weak.

- **If this is new to you:** Use real numbers from somewhere real, even if they are small. An invented example teaches you nothing you can trust.

lessons.title: Working with people
lessons.summary: Delegating, following up, and handling it when someone does not deliver.
objectives: You will delegate a task with a clear outcome and date
You will follow up without nagging
You will handle one missed deadline
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Delegate: say the outcome, the date and who decides — not the method
- Agree one check-in point in advance
- Practise the conversation when it is late: ask what is blocking, not why they failed

## Understand it

As soon as a business has more than one person, results depend on **working through others**. Two skills matter most: **delegating** and **following up**.

**Delegating well — say three things, clearly:**

1. **The outcome** — what "done" looks like. "All 40 members' forms checked and missing details listed."
2. **The date** — when it is due. "By Thursday 4 pm."
3. **Who decides** — what they can decide alone, and what they must check with you. "You can call parents directly; check with me before changing anyone's class."

**Do not dictate the method** unless it truly matters (safety, legal requirements). People who choose their own method own the result, and often find better ways.

**Agree one check-in point in advance** — "Let's look at it together on Tuesday." Agreed check-ins feel like support; surprise checking feels like distrust.

**When it is late:** ask **what is blocking**, not **why** it is late.

- "Why isn't this done?" invites excuses and defensiveness.
- "What's blocking it? What do you need?" invites problem-solving — and often reveals a real obstacle you can remove (missing information, unclear priority, too much other work).

Then agree a new date and what will change.

**Give credit publicly**, criticism privately. People work harder for leaders who notice their work.

## Key words

- **Delegation:** giving someone responsibility for a task
- **Outcome:** the result that defines 'done'
- **Decision rights:** what someone may decide alone
- **Check-in:** an agreed point to review progress

lessons.title: The one number
lessons.summary: Choosing the measure that tells you whether it is working.
objectives: You will choose one measure before acting
You will state the number that would mean failure
You will name a vanity metric
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Pick the one number that would show it worked
- State in advance what number would mean stop
- Spot the flattering numbers that tell you nothing

## Understand it

Businesses drown in numbers. Strategy needs **one number** that shows whether the thing you are doing is working.

**Pick the one number that would show it worked.** It should be linked directly to the goal:

- Goal: more repeat customers → **% of customers who return within a month**.
- Goal: faster service → **average minutes from order to delivery**.
- Goal: profitable new product → **profit per week** from it (not sales).

**State in advance what number would mean stop.** Before starting: "If fewer than 30 people sign up in the first month, we stop the evening class and try a weekend one." Deciding beforehand protects you from the very human tendency to keep going with a failing idea because you have invested in it (the **sunk cost** trap).

**Spot the flattering numbers that tell you nothing:**

- **Total registrations ever** — always goes up; says nothing about this month.
- **Followers, views, likes** — do not pay the bills.
- **Revenue without costs** — busy is not the same as profitable.
- **Averages hiding extremes** — average delivery time 30 minutes, but one in five takes two hours.

These are sometimes called **vanity metrics**.

**Track it regularly** — weekly is usually right — on a simple chart. A trend tells you far more than a single figure.

## Key words

- **Key metric:** the one number that shows whether the goal is met
- **Stop condition:** a result decided in advance that means stop
- **Sunk cost:** money or time already spent that cannot be recovered
- **Vanity metric:** a flattering number that does not show real progress

lessons.title: What goes wrong
lessons.summary: Risk: naming the three things most likely to break, before they do.
objectives: You will list the three most likely failures
You will say what you would do about each
You will name which you accept
lessons.body:
## What to do

- List what could go wrong, then rank by likelihood and damage
- For the top three, decide: prevent, prepare, or accept
- Write down what you are accepting, explicitly

## Understand it

Every business faces risks. Good managers do not pretend otherwise — they **list them, rank them, and decide** what to do about each.

**1. List what could go wrong.** Think broadly:

- **Money** — a customer does not pay; prices rise; cash runs out.
- **People** — a key person leaves or falls ill.
- **Supply** — a supplier fails; goods are delayed at the port.
- **Operations** — power cuts, equipment breaks, fire, theft.
- **Legal and reputation** — a food safety complaint, a data breach, a bad review.
- **External** — fuel scarcity, currency changes, flooding, new regulations.

**2. Rank by likelihood and damage.** Score each 1–5 for how likely and how bad; multiply. The highest scores need attention first. (A **risk matrix** shows this as a grid.)

**3. For the top three, decide:**

- **Prevent** — reduce the likelihood (lock up stock; train a second person; test the generator weekly).
- **Prepare** — reduce the damage if it happens (insurance; a backup supplier; a cash reserve; backups of records).
- **Accept** — if it is unlikely or cheap, live with it.

**4. Write down what you are accepting — explicitly.** "We accept the risk of a two-day power cut; we will lose some stock, and we've decided a second generator is not worth it." Writing it down turns an accident into a decision, and lets others challenge it.

A **pre-mortem** helps: imagine the project has failed, and ask "what went wrong?"

## Key words

- **Risk:** something that might happen and cause harm
- **Likelihood × impact:** a simple way to rank risks
- **Mitigation:** action that reduces a risk
- **Pre-mortem:** imagining failure in advance to find risks

lessons.title: Pitch and defend
lessons.summary: A real proposal with real numbers, defended under questioning.
objectives: You will pitch a proposal with checked numbers
You will state your measure and your risks
You will answer three hard questions
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Pitch: the problem, the evidence, the numbers, the measure, the risks
- Say what you will not do
- Take three hard questions and answer with evidence

## Understand it

A **pitch** asks people — investors, a bank, a grant panel, a manager, a partner — to back an idea. A strong pitch is built on everything in this course.

**The structure:**

1. **The problem** — who has it, and how badly. One real example beats a general claim.
2. **The evidence** — what you learnt from customers (week 2): what they said and, more importantly, what they did.
3. **The numbers** — costs, margin, break-even (weeks 3 and 7), with **real prices**.
4. **The measure** — the one number that will show it works, and what number would mean stop (week 10).
5. **The risks** — the top three and what you will do about each (week 11). Naming risks yourself builds trust; hiding them destroys it when they are discovered.
6. **What you will not do** (week 8) — shows focus and judgement.
7. **The ask** — exactly what you need: money, time, a decision, a partner.

**Taking hard questions:**

- Listen to the **whole** question before answering.
- Answer with **evidence**: "We spoke to 25 parents; 18 had paid for a similar class before."
- If you do not know: "I don't know yet — here's how I'll find out." Never invent numbers.
- Do not get defensive — questions mean they are taking the idea seriously.

**Rehearse** out loud, with a timer, in front of people who will ask difficult questions.

## Key words

- **Pitch:** a short presentation asking people to back an idea
- **The ask:** exactly what you want from the audience
- **Due diligence:** the checks backers make before committing
